message.content: {"summary":"A well-structured, fluent report that clearly identifies the ethical issues and stakeholders, and builds a balanced argument toward a well-supported 'do not ship' conclusion. Your use of the EA Code of Ethics and case studies (NHS, VW) is effective. To reach the top band, deepen stakeholder-specific recommendations, add quantitative evidence, and incorporate visual elements.","next_steps":["Differentiate your decision-making recommendations for each stakeholder (e.g., the health department, chip contract company), not just Rachel and her company.","Strengthen arguments with quantitative evidence such as fine amounts, defect/failure rates, or recall costs, alongside your qualitative case studies.","Add visual elements (e.g., a stakeholder-interest table or decision-flow figure) and complete reference details (URL/access date for [3], full authorship for [1]) in consistent IEEE style."],"criteria":{"C1":"Excellent work: you identified several ethical issues (public safety, integrity, reputation, business survival), linked them to engineering design, and clearly demonstrated both the organisational context and stakeholder interests in your Introduction. This is already at the top level — maintain this breadth in future work.","C2":"Your arguments for and against shipping are objective and reasonably deep, and your conclusion is clear. To reach Excellent, provide decision-making recommendations for several different stakeholders — e.g., how the health department or chip company should act — rather than focusing mainly on Rachel's company.","C3":"Your body is logically structured, moving from business to safety, integrity and reputation, and your conclusion is well supported. For the top level, demonstrate a fully systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders, and tighten internally inconsistent arguments (e.g., the third 'for' argument in your Discussion).","C4":"Good use of four relevant references, including the NHS IT-failure case, the VW scandal, and the EA Code of Ethics. To reach Excellent, add quantitative evidence (fines, failure rates, costs) and broaden your research; also reconsider the NHS analogy, as it concerns IT system failures rather than knowingly shipped defective hardware.","C5":"Your writing is fluent with only minor errors (e.g., 'The economic benefits of could very well be the difference'), but no figures, tables or visual elements were used, and some references are incomplete ([3] lacks URL/access details; [1] lacks an author). Adding visuals and polishing IEEE formatting would lift this criterion."}}
